newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - SCANDINAVIAN INSURERS.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - SCANDINAVIAN INSURERS.

text.p: The decision by Swedish insurer WASA to sell the bulk of its British subsidiary's business to fellow Swedish insurer SIRIUS International is the latest manifestation of a stay-at-home trend among Scandinavian insurers.

In recent years several Swedish insurers have reduced their international presence, partly in response to reinsurance losses and partly because of group issues in Sweden. Skandia in particular was weakened by the scramble to establish a Nordic giant insurer. After the Danish insurer, Hafnia, and the Norwegian insurer, Uni-Storebrand, failed to take over Skandia in 1992, the latter attempted - unsuccessfully - to acquire Hafnia.

The domestic Swedish market is served by Swedish companies almost to the exclusion of foreign groups. The latter have only a 2.8% market share, one of the lowest proportions in Europe. Finland is similar.

One reason for this is the small population - 8.9m - relative to some other European countries, which combined with the relative maturity of the market does not provide a strong incentive to foreign groups to invest in Sweden.

WASA writes relatively little international business. The British subsidiary, WASA International (UK) Insurance Company, estimates its gross income for the 1997 underwriting year around 22m. It concentrates on niche lines of business including accident and health and property.

Sirius is going against the trend. Along with Skandia it has a larger international presence. It has a finite risk reinsurer, Scandinavian Re, in Bermuda, and the WASA deal indicates an intention to boost its London market presence. SIRIUS already has a branch in London of which Lisbeth Sarkozi, managing director of WASA UK, will become general manager.
